# A picture of a learning system

## Two parts

Here is about the simplest picture of a thing that learns.

- **Perception** takes things in from the world.
- **Processing** does something with what came in.

Information enters at one end, gets worked on, and beliefs come out the other.

## The division of labour

Each part has one job.

Perception does not reason. It delivers.

Processing does not look. It works on whatever it was handed.

. . .

That tidiness is what makes the picture attractive, and it is also what we will spend the rest of today poking at.

## Why start here

Almost every view we meet this term is a modification of this picture: adding a part, splitting a part, or denying that the parts come apart.

So it is worth having in view, including the reasons to doubt it.

# The picture is not just ours

## Bayesian machinery

Very roughly, this is the shape of a Bayesian system.

You start with some assignment of confidence. Evidence arrives. A rule tells you how to change your confidence in the light of it.

. . .

Evidence coming in is the perception half. The updating rule is the processing half. The rule never gathers anything, and the evidence never reasons.

## Machine learning, with hedges

The picture is not foreign to a good deal of contemporary machine learning either, where something turns inputs into a representation and something else computes over the representation.

The analogy is loose and you should not lean on it hard. But the two-part shape recurs, which is a reason to take it seriously and a reason to ask what it leaves out.

# You can see the join in Holmes

## The reading

The two pages you read are a single scene, and they divide exactly down this line.

First he gathers. Then he concludes.

## Gathering

> Sherlock Holmes was transformed when he was hot upon such a scent as this. Men who had only known the quiet thinker and logician of Baker Street would have failed to recognise him.

He crawls over the ground with a lens. He is fast, silent, and not talking to anybody.

## The tell

Notice what Doyle does there. The two parts are not just doing different work; they *look* different from outside.

> his nostrils seemed to dilate with a purely animal lust for the chase

The quiet logician of Baker Street is the other mode. Same man, different behaviour, and Watson can tell which one is running.

## Concluding

Back at the carriage the animal is gone and the expositor is back:

> Is a tall man, left-handed, limps with the right leg, wears thick-soled shooting-boots and a grey cloak, smokes Indian cigars, uses a cigar-holder, and carries a blunt pen-knife in his pocket.

Nothing new comes in during that speech. He is working on what he already has.

## He names the two himself

Earlier in the story, before the part you read:

> I only quote this as a trivial example of observation and inference. Therein lies my métier.

Observation and inference. Perception and processing.

. . .

He is describing our diagram, seventy years before anybody drew it.

# Reasons to doubt it

## Where might it go wrong

Three places, and we will take them in order.

- Something might be neither perception nor processing.
- Processing might not be one thing.
- The line between the two might not be sharp.

## Something that is neither

Suppose some of what you know did not come in through the senses and was not worked out from what did.

That is the old idea of **innate ideas**: knowledge you arrive with. Plato has Meno's slave boy produce geometry he was never taught. Descartes thinks some ideas are stamped in. Chomsky argues no child hears enough language to explain what they end up knowing.

## The same worry, in the machinery

The Bayesian version is sharper, and it is not historical at all.

Before any evidence arrives, the system has to start somewhere. That starting point is not something perception delivered, and it is not something processing computed.

. . .

Hold on to that. It comes back with a vengeance on Thursday.

# Processing is not one thing

## Split it

The obvious first cut is the one you have already met.

- **Deduction**, where the conclusion is already settled by what you have.
- **Induction**, where you reach past what you have to something new.

Tuesday was entirely deduction. The clues forced the verdicts, and finding them added nothing.

## Deduction is safe and gives nothing new

That sounds like a complaint, and partly it is. But safety buys two things worth having.

## One: arguments chain

Valid steps compose. Put a thousand together and the conclusion is as good as the premises.

Modern machines chain billions of steps. If each step were merely very reliable rather than valid, a tiny error rate would compound until the output was worthless.

. . .

Deduction is the only kind of inference you can do that much of and still trust the end.

## Two: you can check the form

A valid argument is valid because of its shape, not its subject.

So you can check it without understanding it. Something that has no idea what the sentences mean can still verify that the reasoning has the right form.

That is what makes proof-checking software possible, and it is why deduction is the part of reasoning we have been able to hand over.

## And you could cut further

Deduction and induction is a first cut, not the last one.

Is memory a third thing, or storage attached to the other two? Is taking somebody's word for it a way of processing, or a second way of taking things in?

. . .

We spend three weeks on that second question later in the term.

# Maybe the line is not sharp

## Cognitive penetration

The picture assumes perception hands over its results without caring what you already think.

Some philosophers and psychologists deny this. The claim is that what you believe, expect or want can shape what you actually see, not merely what you conclude from it.

## Why it matters, and why we stop here

If it is right, the diagram does not just need more boxes. The arrow runs both ways, and perception stops being an independent check on what you believe.

. . .

The debate is live and technical: Susanna Siegel and Nicholas Silins on one side of it, Chaz Firestone and Brian Scholl arguing in *Behavioral and Brain Sciences* that cognition does not affect perception at all.

We are not doing it in this course. You should know it exists, and that our tidy picture is contested at its foundation.

# Where this goes

## What we have

A two-part picture, three ways of doubting it, and one part now split into the safe half and the risky half.

## Thursday

We take the risky half seriously and ask the obvious question about it.

You have seen a thousand ravens and every one was black. What exactly entitles you to anything about the next one?

. . .

The answer is stranger than it looks.
